source.title: The Prophet
source.attribution: Kahlil Gibran, The Prophet, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Close couples still need room to be themselves
cards.body:
Gibran's advice on marriage is to be together without fusing into one person. Share your lives, but let each partner keep their own interests, friends and quiet time, like two strings on the same instrument that each make their own sound.

Couples sometimes feel that wanting space means something is wrong. Often the opposite is true: people who keep growing as individuals bring more to the relationship. A solo hobby, a separate weekend with friends or an evening apart can strengthen the bond rather than weaken it.
cards.quote: But let there be spaces in your togetherness
cards.apply_it: Ask your partner (or reflect, if single) about one interest each of you would like more personal time for, and plan room for it.

quiz.question: What does Gibran recommend for a marriage?
quiz.explanation: He advises closeness with room for each person, like separate strings playing the same music.

cards.title: Your children are not copies of you
cards.body:
Gibran reminds parents that children come through them but don't belong to them. You can give them love, a home and guidance, but not your thoughts; they will grow into a future you can't fully see.

It is tempting to steer kids toward the career, hobbies or beliefs you wish you had. Gibran suggests the opposite: learn from them and let them become themselves. That might mean supporting a path you wouldn't pick, while still providing a stable base from which they can launch.
cards.quote: You may strive to be like them, but seek not to make them like you.
cards.apply_it: Ask a child (or younger person) in your life what they are excited about right now, and listen without steering.

quiz.question: What does Gibran advise parents about their children?
options: Give them your love but not your thoughts
quiz.explanation: Children have their own thoughts; parents can be like them but shouldn't try to make them copies.

cards.title: Work done with care feeds people; work done with indifference shortchanges them
cards.body:
Gibran's chapter on work ends with a striking claim: work is love made visible. Bread baked with indifference is bitter and only half satisfies.

In any job, people can feel whether you cared: the email that actually answers the question, the code with clear names, the meal made with attention. Care doesn't require loving every task. It means imagining the person who will use what you make and doing it as if they mattered, because they do. That attitude often turns routine work into something meaningful.
cards.quote: For if you bake bread with indifference, you bake a bitter bread that feeds but half man’s hunger.
cards.apply_it: Before your next routine task, picture the specific person who will use the result. Do one extra thing that would make it better for them.

quiz.question: What happens, in Gibran's image, when bread is baked with indifference?
options: It feeds only half of a person's hunger
quiz.explanation: Indifferent work falls short; Gibran calls work done with care 'love made visible'.

cards.title: Sorrow and joy grow from the same places in your life
cards.body:
Gibran writes that joy and sorrow are inseparable. What makes you happy, a person, a place, a calling, is exactly what can later make you grieve. And the deeper sorrow carves into you, the more joy you are able to hold.

This is a useful lens in hard times. Grief over a lost relationship or a pet shows how much they mattered. Painful experiences can also make you more sensitive to small pleasures afterwards. Allowing both feelings, instead of numbing one, keeps you able to feel the other.
cards.quote: The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.
cards.apply_it: Think of something you have grieved. Write one sentence on what it shows you value, and one way you can honour that today.

quiz.question: What does Gibran say about the relationship between joy and sorrow?
options: Sorrow should be avoided at all costs
They are inseparable, coming from the same source
quiz.explanation: He sees them as two sides of the same well; sorrow can deepen our capacity for joy.

cards.title: Steer with reason, move with passion; you need both
cards.body:
Gibran compares reason and passion to the rudder and sails of a ship. Without sails, you go nowhere; without a rudder, you drift or crash. Reason alone confines, and passion without guidance burns itself out.

People often treat feelings and logic as enemies. In practice, good decisions use both: emotion tells you what you care about and gives energy, while reasoning chooses the route. Next time you're torn, ask what your feelings are telling you and what your judgement says, then look for a path that honours both.
cards.quote: For reason, ruling alone, is a force confining; and passion, unattended, is a flame that burns to its own destruction.
cards.apply_it: For one decision you're facing, write what your feelings want and what your reasoning says. Look for an option that respects both.

quiz.question: In Gibran's image, what are reason and passion?
options: The rudder and sails of a ship
quiz.explanation: Reason steers and passion propels; each fails without the other.

cards.title: Seek friends to share life with, not just to kill time
cards.body:
Gibran draws a distinction between seeing a friend with 'hours to kill' and with 'hours to live'. One treats friendship as filler for boredom; the other brings your real self and full attention.

It's easy to meet friends while half-scrolling, or only when there is nothing better to do. Gibran asks for more: give your friend your best, share your good tides and not only your low ones, and enjoy laughter and small pleasures together. Presence, not time spent, is what deepens a friendship.
cards.quote: For what is your friend that you should seek him with hours to kill?
cards.apply_it: Next time you meet a friend, put your phone away for the whole visit and share one good thing in your life, not just problems.

quiz.question: What does Gibran mean by seeking a friend with 'hours to live'?
options: Bringing real presence instead of using them to fill empty time
Spending as many hours as possible together
quiz.explanation: He contrasts filling idle time with truly living alongside a friend.

cards.title: Notice when you're talking only to avoid sitting with your thoughts
cards.body:
Gibran observes that we often talk when we are no longer at peace with our own thoughts. Some people seek out chatty company because silence would leave them face to face with themselves.

Today the same urge reaches for podcasts, calls or scrolling the moment a quiet minute appears. Constant noise can crowd out real thinking. Spending a little time in silence, on a walk or a commute without audio, lets thoughts settle and makes your later words more considered.
cards.quote: And in much of your talking, thinking is half murdered.
cards.apply_it: Take a ten-minute walk or commute today with no audio and no phone. Notice what thoughts come up.

quiz.question: According to Gibran, what often happens to thinking in much of our talking?
quiz.explanation: He suggests that constant talk can crowd out thought, often as a way to escape our own company.

cards.title: Real love will stretch and change you, not only comfort you
cards.body:
Gibran's prophet warns that love is not a soft place to hide. The same love that lifts you up will also expose your weak spots, shake your habits and ask you to grow. He compares it to a gardener who both tends a tree and cuts it back.

This helps when a relationship gets hard. Friction does not always mean something is wrong; often it means you are being asked to become more patient, honest or generous. People who want only the pleasant side of love, Gibran says, end up living a smaller life, laughing and crying only halfway.
cards.quote: Even as he is for your growth so is he for your pruning.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent tension with someone you love. What is it asking you to grow in: patience, honesty or letting go?

quiz.question: According to Gibran, what does love do besides bringing joy?
options: It keeps you safe from all hurt
It prunes and reshapes you so you grow
It lets you control the other person
It removes the need for effort
quiz.explanation: Gibran pictures love as a gardener: it helps you grow but also cuts back what holds you back.

cards.title: Love does not own the other person
cards.body:
Gibran insists that love neither possesses nor wants to be possessed. It gives itself and is complete in itself. That rules out treating a partner, child or friend as property you control.

Possessiveness often disguises itself as care: checking phones, deciding who someone may see, needing to know where they are every minute. The prophet's view suggests a test. If your love needs to hold the other person tightly to feel secure, what you feel may be fear more than love. Love that trusts gives the other room and still stays close.
cards.quote: Love possesses not nor would it be possessed;
cards.apply_it: Notice one way you try to control someone you love. What would trusting them in that area look like this week?

quiz.question: What is Gibran's view of possession in love?
options: Love should own the beloved completely
Love neither possesses nor wants to be possessed
quiz.explanation: He says love possesses not nor would it be possessed; it is enough in itself.

cards.title: Your time and attention are worth more than your money
cards.body:
When a rich man asks about giving, the prophet answers that handing over possessions is a small gift. The real gift is giving of yourself: your time, your skill, your attention, your care.

This is freeing for anyone without much money. A visit to someone who is lonely, an hour teaching a younger colleague, or truly listening to a friend can matter more than a cash gift. It also challenges those with money: writing a cheque is easy, but showing up costs something real, and people feel the difference.
cards.quote: It is when you give of yourself that you truly give.
cards.apply_it: Choose one person this week and give them an hour of undivided time: a visit, a call or help with a task.

quiz.question: According to the prophet, when do you truly give?
options: When you give large sums of money
When you give only to the deserving
quiz.explanation: He says possessions are a small gift; giving of yourself is the true gift.

cards.title: Constant fear of running short is its own kind of poverty
cards.body:
Gibran points out that we often cling to possessions out of fear of tomorrow. Then he turns the idea over: dread of need is already a form of need. Someone with a full well who still fears thirst is never satisfied.

Planning and saving are wise. But if no amount ever feels safe, money stops serving you and starts ruling you. You can't enjoy what you have, and you can't share it. Notice when caution has turned into anxiety, and set a clear 'enough' so your savings bring peace rather than more worry.
cards.quote: And what is fear of need but need itself?
cards.apply_it: Write down the amount of savings that would genuinely make you feel secure. Is your worry tracking that number, or running on its own?

quiz.question: What does Gibran say about the fear of need?
options: Fear of need is itself a kind of need
It is the best motivation to work
It disappears once you are rich
It is the same as wisdom
quiz.explanation: He asks, 'what is fear of need but need itself?', pointing out that anxiety about lack keeps you poor in spirit.

cards.title: Give while you are alive to see the good it does
cards.body:
The prophet reminds his listeners that everything they own will one day be given away, whether they choose to or not. So why not give now, while the choice and the joy are yours rather than your heirs'?

Many people plan to be generous 'later', once they have more. Later may not come, or may come when they cannot see the results. Helping a niece with school fees now, supporting a cause you care about this year, or passing on tools you no longer use lets you share in the good it does.
cards.quote: Therefore give now, that the season of giving may be yours and not your inheritors’.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you plan to give 'someday', whether money, an item or your help, and give it this month.

quiz.question: Why does the prophet urge people to give now?
options: Because all you have will be given away someday anyway
Because giving later is not allowed
quiz.explanation: All you have shall some day be given, so give now and let the season of giving be yours.

cards.title: Don't make people prove they deserve your help
cards.body:
People often say they will give, 'but only to the deserving'. Gibran answers that the trees in an orchard do not check who deserves their fruit. Anyone worthy of receiving life itself is worthy of a little from you.

He also warns about the cost of interrogating people in need: making them strip away their pride so you can judge their worth. Some caution is sensible, but humiliating questions do real harm. When you can help, help with dignity. Ask what someone needs, not what they did to end up needing it.
cards.quote: You often say, ‘I would give, but only to the deserving.’
cards.apply_it: Next time you help someone, skip the questions about how they got into trouble and ask only what would help most.

quiz.question: What does Gibran use to challenge the idea of giving only to the deserving?
options: A king who rewards loyal servants
A merchant who checks every account
The trees in an orchard and the flocks in a pasture
A judge who weighs the evidence
quiz.explanation: He says the trees in your orchard and the flocks in your pasture don't give only to the deserving; they give that they may live.

cards.title: Accept help gracefully, without drowning in a sense of debt
cards.body:
The prophet speaks to receivers, which he says we all are. Don't load yourself with such a heavy sense of owing that it becomes a yoke on you and on the person who gave. Rise with the giver instead, as if the gift were wings for you both.

Many people find receiving harder than giving. They refuse help, repay instantly, or apologise endlessly. That can quietly insult the giver, as if their kindness came with a bill. A warm, simple thank-you, and later passing kindness on to someone else, honours a gift better than anxious repayment.
cards.quote: And you receivers⁠—and you are all receivers⁠—assume no weight of gratitude, lest you lay a yoke upon yourself and upon him who gives.
cards.apply_it: The next time someone helps you, say a warm thank-you and resist the urge to repay immediately or apologise.

quiz.question: What does the prophet warn receivers against?
options: Carrying a heavy sense of debt that burdens both people
quiz.explanation: He warns that being overmindful of your debt lays a yoke on you and the giver.

cards.title: No honest work is beneath anyone
cards.body:
People in Orphalese ranked work: the sculptor above the ploughman, the painter above the sandal-maker. The prophet rejects this. The wind, he says, speaks no more sweetly to the giant oaks than to the smallest blade of grass. Greatness lies in doing your work with love, not in its status.

This matters in societies that look down on manual or service work. The cleaner, the farmer, the mechanic and the cook keep life running. Respecting all honest work makes you a better colleague and boss, and it frees you from shame about work you may need to do on the way to something else.
cards.quote: the wind speaks not more sweetly to the giant oaks than to the least of all the blades of grass;
cards.apply_it: Thank someone whose work is often overlooked, such as a cleaner, guard or driver, by name this week.

quiz.question: How does the prophet respond to the idea that some work is nobler than other work?
options: He agrees artists are greater than farmers
He says greatness comes from working with love, not from the type of work
He says only religious work matters
He says all work is a curse
quiz.explanation: He says the wind speaks as sweetly to grass as to oaks; greatness is turning work into something made sweeter by love.

cards.title: Knowledge is wasted until you put it to work
cards.body:
Gibran gives a short chain: desire is blind without knowledge, knowledge is empty without work, and work is empty without love. Each link needs the next.

It is easy to collect knowledge: courses, books, videos, advice. But until you act on it, it changes nothing. The reverse also holds: effort without understanding goes in circles, and effort without care turns hollow. A practical check is to ask of everything you learn: where will I use this? Then do it, and do it with care for the people it serves.
cards.quote: And all knowledge is vain save when there is work,
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you learned recently and use it in a real task within the next 48 hours.

quiz.question: In Gibran's chain, what makes knowledge worthwhile?
options: Work that puts it into practice
quiz.explanation: He says all knowledge is vain save when there is work, and all work is empty save when there is love.

cards.title: Comfort arrives as a guest and can end up as your master
cards.body:
The prophet asks what people keep in their houses: peace, memories, beauty? Or only comfort, and the craving for more of it? He describes that craving as something that arrives as a guest, becomes a host, then becomes a master.

Comfort is not bad. But if every choice is about avoiding effort, it slowly shrinks your life: you skip the course, the early start, the hard conversation, the trip. Gibran wants your home to be a mast that carries you forward, not an anchor. Check whether your comforts still serve your bigger goals.
cards.quote: Or have you only comfort, and the lust for comfort, that stealthy thing that enters the house a guest, and then becomes a host, and then a master?
cards.apply_it: Name one comfort that has started to crowd out something you care about. Set one small limit on it this week.

quiz.question: How does the prophet describe the craving for comfort?
options: A guest that becomes a host and then a master
A reward you should never question
A sign of a successful life
A harmless habit with no effect
quiz.explanation: He says the lust for comfort enters as a guest, becomes a host, and then a master.

cards.title: Trade fairly, and make sure nobody leaves the market empty-handed
cards.body:
Speaking to a merchant, the prophet says exchange can create plenty for everyone, but only if it is done with love and kindly justice. Otherwise it leads some to greed and others to hunger.

He ends with a striking instruction: before you leave the market, make sure no one has gone home with empty hands. For a business owner that might mean fair prices, honest weights, paying suppliers on time, or helping a struggling neighbour trader. Good trade is not a contest with one winner. Markets that leave many people hungry eventually fail everyone.
cards.quote: And before you leave the market place, see that no one has gone his way with empty hands.
cards.apply_it: Review one regular deal you make, with a supplier, customer or worker. Is it fair to both sides? Adjust one thing if not.

quiz.question: According to the prophet, what happens when trade lacks love and kindly justice?
options: It leads some to greed and others to hunger
quiz.explanation: He says unless the exchange is in love and kindly justice, it will lead some to greed and others to hunger.

cards.title: When something goes wrong, examine the whole system, not just the person
cards.body:
In his talk on crime, the prophet uses an image from weaving. Good and bad are woven together like black and white thread. When the black thread breaks, a good weaver looks at the whole cloth, and at the loom too.

In a workplace this means that when a mistake happens, blaming one person is rarely the full answer. What training did they get? Were the targets unrealistic? Did the process invite error? Looking at the loom does not excuse wrongdoing, but it fixes the conditions that will produce the next failure too.
cards.quote: And when the black thread breaks, the weaver shall look into the whole cloth, and he shall examine the loom also.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent mistake at work or home. List two conditions that made it more likely, not only who made it.

quiz.question: What does the weaver do when the black thread breaks?
options: Blames the thread and moves on
Examines the whole cloth and the loom
quiz.explanation: The weaver looks into the whole cloth and examines the loom also, the system that produced the break.

cards.title: Don't turn your own limits into rules for everyone else
cards.body:
Gibran describes people who make laws out of their own limits: the person who cannot dance and so hates dancers, the ox who loves his yoke and calls free deer lawless, the guest who overate and now calls every feast wrong. They stand in the sun with their backs to it and see only their own shadows.

We all do this sometimes. The person who never travelled scorns those who move abroad; the one who gave up on a dream mocks people still chasing theirs. Before condemning someone's choices, ask whether your objection is a real principle or just the outline of your own fear or disappointment.
cards.quote: They see only their shadows, and their shadows are their laws.
cards.apply_it: Think of a choice by someone else that irritates you. Is it actually wrong, or does it just remind you of something you gave up?

quiz.question: What do the people 'with their backs to the sun' do, according to Gibran?
options: Make their own shadows into laws for others
Follow the sun wherever it goes
quiz.explanation: They see only their shadows, and their shadows are their laws: they turn their own limits into rules.

cards.title: Much of your fear lives in you, not in the thing you fear
cards.body:
On freedom, the prophet makes a sharp point: if there is a fear you want to drive away, its seat is in your heart, not in the hand of the thing you fear. The boss, the exam or the phone call does not carry the fear around; you do.

This does not mean real dangers are imaginary. It means the part of fear that keeps you awake, rehearsing disasters, is something you can work on directly. Naming the fear, checking the actual odds, and preparing a plan often shrinks it, while the outside situation stays exactly the same.
cards.quote: And if it is a fear you would dispel, the seat of that fear is in your heart and not in the hand of the feared.
cards.apply_it: Write down one fear that keeps returning. Next to it, write what is actually likely and one step you could take to prepare.

quiz.question: Where does the prophet say the seat of fear is?
options: In the person or thing you fear
In the laws of the city
quiz.explanation: He says the seat of that fear is in your heart and not in the hand of the feared.

cards.title: Pain can be the shell cracking so understanding can grow
cards.body:
Asked about pain, the prophet compares it to the breaking of a shell or the stone of a fruit, which has to split so the living heart inside can reach the sun. Hard experiences often break open old certainties so we can understand more.

He also asks us to accept the seasons of the heart as we accept the seasons over the fields, watching calmly through the winters of grief. This is not a call to seek suffering or to ignore it. It is a way of carrying it: asking, when the worst has passed, what the pain has opened up in you.
cards.quote: Your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.
cards.apply_it: Recall a painful period that is now behind you. Write one thing you understand now that you did not understand before it.

quiz.question: What image does the prophet use for pain?
options: A wall that should never be crossed
A shell breaking open to free what is inside
quiz.explanation: He calls pain the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding, like a fruit stone splitting open.

cards.title: Say you have found a truth, not the truth
cards.body:
Speaking on self-knowledge, the prophet offers a small change of wording with large effects: don't say 'I have found the truth'; say 'I have found a truth'. The self, and life, are too vast to fit into one discovery.

This habit protects you from the closed mind that comes with certainty. You can hold strong views and still leave room to learn more. In arguments it changes the tone: 'this is what I've found' invites conversation, while 'this is the truth' ends it. It also lets you change your mind without feeling you have lost face.
cards.quote: Say not, ‘I have found the truth,’ but rather, ‘I have found a truth.’
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, swap 'the truth is' for 'what I've found is', and notice how the conversation changes.

quiz.question: What wording does the prophet recommend?
options: I have found the only path
Truth cannot be found at all
quiz.explanation: He says not to claim 'the truth' but 'a truth', because the self is a sea boundless and measureless.

cards.title: A good teacher leads you to your own thinking, not into theirs
cards.body:
The prophet says a wise teacher does not invite you into the house of his wisdom. He leads you to the threshold of your own mind. No one can hand you their understanding; they can only help wake up what is already half-awake in you.

This is useful whether you are learning or teaching. As a learner, don't just copy a mentor's answers; ask how they think, then work it out yourself. As a parent, manager or teacher, ask questions that help others reason, rather than giving answers they will forget. Understanding sticks when people reach it themselves.
cards.quote: If he is indeed wise he does not bid you enter the house of his wisdom, but rather leads you to the threshold of your own mind.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone asks you for help, ask them two questions about what they think before you offer your answer.

quiz.question: According to the prophet, what does a wise teacher do?
options: Leads you to the threshold of your own mind
Tells you exactly what to believe
quiz.explanation: A wise teacher leads you to the threshold of your own mind rather than into the house of his own wisdom.

cards.title: Share your good times with friends, not only your troubles
cards.body:
The prophet tells the young man to give his best to his friend: if your friend must know the low tide of your life, let them know the high tide as well.

Some friendships drift into being only about problems. One person calls when things go wrong and disappears when life is good. Others hide their successes from friends out of modesty or fear of envy. Gibran's advice is to let friends share the whole of you: the wins, the plans and the celebrations as well as the struggles. That balance is what keeps a friendship from becoming just a support line.
cards.quote: If he must know the ebb of your tide, let him know its flood also.
cards.apply_it: Call a friend you usually contact only when something is wrong, and share some good news or a happy moment instead.

quiz.question: What does the prophet ask you to share with your friend besides your low points?
options: Your high points too, the flood as well as the ebb
quiz.explanation: He says if your friend must know the ebb of your tide, let them know its flood also.

cards.title: Slow progress is still progress: even the limping go forward
cards.body:
In his talk on good and evil, the prophet is gentle with people who move slowly. You are good when you walk to your goal with bold, firm steps. But you are not bad when you go there limping. Even those who limp do not go backward.

This is a useful antidote to all-or-nothing thinking. If you can't study for two hours, twenty minutes still counts. If your savings grow slowly, they are still growing. Halting progress feels discouraging, but direction matters more than speed. Keep facing the goal and keep moving, however awkwardly.
cards.quote: Even those who limp go not backward.
cards.apply_it: Pick a goal you have stalled on and do the smallest possible step today, even five minutes.

quiz.question: What does the prophet say about those who move toward their goal limping?
options: They still do not go backward
They must be carried by others
quiz.explanation: He says you are not evil when you go limping, for even those who limp go not backward.

cards.title: Don't shame people for what life has taken from them
cards.body:
The prophet closes his talk on good and evil with a quiet line: the truly good do not ask the naked where their garment is, nor the homeless what happened to their house.

When someone is struggling, people often start with questions that feel like blame: why didn't you save, why did you take that job, why did you trust him? Even when meant kindly, these questions add shame to hardship. Gibran also warns that those who long for much shouldn't scold those who move more slowly. Meet people where they are. Help first; the lessons, if any, can wait.
cards.quote: For the truly good ask not the naked, ‘Where is your garment?’ nor the houseless, ‘What has befallen your house?’
cards.apply_it: Next time someone tells you about a setback, respond with 'How can I help?' before any 'Why did you…?'

quiz.question: Which questions do the truly good avoid asking, according to the prophet?
options: What can I do for you?
Where is your garment? What has befallen your house?
quiz.explanation: He says the truly good ask not the naked 'Where is your garment?' nor the houseless 'What has befallen your house?'

cards.title: Remember past joys with gratitude, not regret
cards.body:
Gibran notes that some older people remember the pleasures of their youth with regret, as if they were wrongs done while drunk. He says regret clouds the mind rather than teaching it. Better to remember those pleasures with gratitude, as you would remember a good summer harvest.

This is not about excusing harm you did. It is about the ordinary joys, the trips, friendships, music and fun, that some people later treat as wasted or shameful. Looking back with thanks lets those memories keep nourishing you instead of weighing on you.
cards.quote: But regret is the beclouding of the mind and not its chastisement.
cards.apply_it: Recall a happy period you sometimes look back on with regret. Write three things from it you are thankful for.

quiz.question: How does Gibran suggest remembering past pleasures?
options: With gratitude, as one remembers a summer's harvest
quiz.explanation: He says regret clouds the mind; they should remember their pleasures with gratitude, as the harvest of a summer.

cards.title: You are as strong as your strongest link, not only as weak as your weakest
cards.body:
In his farewell the prophet takes on a common saying: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. That is only half the truth, he says. You are also as strong as your strongest link. Judging you by your smallest deed is like judging the ocean's power by the frailty of its foam.

We often define ourselves, and others, by our worst moments and biggest flaws. Knowing your weak points is useful, but building on your strengths usually takes you further. Ask what you do best, and how you can do more of it.
cards.quote: This is but half the truth. You are also as strong as your strongest link.
cards.apply_it: List your three strongest qualities. Choose one and find a way to use it more in your work or relationships this week.

quiz.question: How does the prophet complete the saying about a chain's weakest link?
options: Your weakest link is all that matters
You are also as strong as your strongest link
Only others can judge your links
quiz.explanation: He says that being as weak as your weakest link is half the truth; you are also as strong as your strongest link.

cards.title: Kindness that admires itself loses its warmth
cards.body:
In his farewell the prophet blesses the people for giving much without knowing they were giving at all. Then he warns that kindness which gazes at itself in a mirror turns to stone, and a good deed that gives itself sweet names becomes the parent of a curse.

We have all seen help given mainly to be seen: the charity photo, the favour that is mentioned again and again. The person helped feels used, and the giver becomes proud. Kindness keeps its warmth when the focus stays on the other person's need, not on how generous you look.
cards.quote: Verily the kindness that gazes upon itself in a mirror turns to stone,
cards.apply_it: Do one kind act this week that nobody will ever know was yours.

quiz.question: What happens, according to the prophet, to kindness that gazes at itself in a mirror?
quiz.explanation: He says the kindness that gazes upon itself in a mirror turns to stone.
